Replace 'How much would you pay for X?' with questions about current costs and allocated budgets

Use 'Why do you bother?' to get from perceived problems to real ones and understand motivations
Use 'What are the implications of that?' to distinguish between critical problems and minor annoyances

actionable_lessons: Ask 'Why do you bother?' to understand customer motivations and goals
Ask 'What are the implications of that?' to distinguish major problems from minor annoyances
Ask 'Talk me through the last time that happened' to observe real workflows instead of opinions
Watch customers perform tasks to see actual problems and inefficiencies, not perceived ones
Ask 'What else have you tried?' to learn about current solutions and switching costs
Ask 'How are you dealing with it now?' to establish price anchors from current spending
Ask 'Where does the money come from?' in B2B to identify the actual budget owner and decision-makers
Ask 'Who else should I talk to?' at the end of every conversation to generate referrals
Ask 'Is there anything else I should have asked?' to fill gaps in understanding
Get deposits or pre-orders rather than asking hypothetical pricing questions
Track whose budget will pay for your solution and who else holds veto power
If someone won't make introductions, either you're being too formal/pitchy/clingy or they don't care about the problem
arguments: People are overly optimistic about what they would do in the future
If a customer truly cared about a problem, they would have already searched for a solution
Value-based pricing requires understanding the customer's financial worldview
Actual commitment (deposits or pre-orders) proves willingness to pay better than stated intentions
definitions: I-will-pay-to-solve-that problems vs that's-kind-of-annoying-but-I-can-deal-with-it problems - distinguishing between problems with big costly implications and those that don't actually matter
Future-promise statement - a verbal commitment without any actual backing action
examples: Finance team requesting messaging tools to save time on spreadsheets - revealed true need was version control, leading to Dropbox-like solution
Customer describing workflow with 'DISASTER' language and yelling, but when asked implications said interns handled it well

key_points: Understanding customer goals is essential before proposing solutions
Distinguish between major problems with costly implications and minor annoyances
Observe actual customer behavior and workflows rather than relying on opinions
